title: Saudi Arabia Says Houthi Attacks Violate Its 2023 Rapprochement With Iran
excerpt: Deputy Minister Rayed Krimly said Iran is arming, training and supporting the Houthis in breach of UN resolutions and the Beijing agreement; Tehran rejected the charge on October 17 and renewed its offer to mediate, which Riyadh said it had not requested.
body:
• Saudi Deputy Minister Rayed Krimly said Iran continues to arm, train and support the Houthis in violation of UN Security Council resolutions and in violation of its commitments under the 2023 Beijing agreement that restored Saudi-Iran ties after seven years.
  • Iran rejected the charge on October 17: Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said Yemen's armed forces act on their own interests and that Tehran has always been ready to help end the hostilities.
  • The Saudi-led coalition said Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport had been targeted 20 times this month, and on October 17 it reported intercepting three drones, two cruise missiles over the Red Sea and a ballistic missile over Yanbu.
  • For travellers: Air India and Air India Express suspended flights to and from Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam until October 20, with full refunds for affected passengers, according to reporting on October 17.

Saudi Arabia has said that Houthi attacks on the kingdom violate the terms of its rapprochement with Iran, in a rare public briefing by Deputy Minister for Public Diplomacy Rayed Krimly that Middle East Eye described as the first public sign that the Yemen war is straining Riyadh's ties with Tehran.

Krimly told journalists that Saudi Arabia believes the latest Houthi escalation was encouraged by Iran. The Vaultz News quoted him as saying: "We think the escalation by the Houthis at this later stage of the conflict is encouraged by Iran."

"Iran continues to arm, train and support the Houthi militia, in violation of United Nations Security Council resolutions."

— Rayed Krimly, Saudi Deputy Minister for Public Diplomacy

The Beijing Agreement at the Centre of the Row

The agreement Krimly cited was reached in Beijing in 2023. It restored diplomatic relations between Saudi Arabia and Iran after a seven-year rupture, and it rested on an expectation that Tehran would use its influence to curb Houthi violence against the kingdom, according to Jawawa, reporting AFP and The Express Tribune coverage of the October 16 briefing.

By naming Iran's support for the Houthis as a breach of that deal, Riyadh moved beyond its usual language about a proxy conflict. Krimly also described attacks on civilian infrastructure as war crimes and put the death toll from the campaign at at least 19 people, including foreign nationals, in the Vaultz News account.

The Attacks Behind the Statement

The briefing followed more than a week of Houthi attacks on Riyadh's international airport, the headquarters of Saudi Aramco, and other aviation, oil and military facilities. A spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition said King Khalid International Airport had been targeted 20 times this month alone.

The fighting has continued since. On Friday, the coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed three drones in southern Saudi Arabia and Riyadh and two cruise missiles over the Red Sea, and had intercepted a ballistic missile over Yanbu, a Red Sea city that is the terminus of a major oil pipeline, Islamabad Post reported.

The same report said the UN Security Council on Thursday condemned Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia and threats to Red Sea shipping. In Aden, two missiles landed inside the airport perimeter on Friday, and a day earlier a missile attack on the presidential palace killed five people and wounded 16.

Iran's Reply, and the Closed Mediation Door

Iran denied any role the next day. "The Islamic Republic of Iran rejects any claim that Iran has played a role in Yemeni (Houthi) operations," Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said, adding that such claims were "not credible to those familiar with relations between Iran and its friends" and that escalation was in no party's interest, according to Islamabad Post.

Krimly closed off one route Tehran had offered. Saudi Arabia had not asked Iran to mediate, he said, and Oman serves as a facilitator of talks with the Houthis, not as a mediator. He said Riyadh had invited the Houthis to meet in Muscat at the start of the current escalation and they had refused, a point also reported by The Daily Jagran.

Krimly added that Saudi Arabia maintained direct communication with both the Houthis and Iran, and that the two countries' foreign ministers had spoken by telephone at least once during the attacks on Riyadh's airport.

What It Means for the Region

The 2023 deal was the main structure keeping Saudi-Iran rivalry contained while Yemen's war, which flared again in July, continued. If Riyadh now treats Houthi strikes as an Iranian treaty violation rather than a Yemeni battlefield problem, its demands shift from a ceasefire in Yemen to concessions from Tehran itself.

For Indians in Saudi Arabia and travellers through Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam, the immediate effect is practical: continued alerts, disrupted flights, and no settlement in sight while the Houthis refuse talks in Muscat.
